items.title: Dalla metro alla palestra, una giornata con gli OpenDots 2 di Shokz agganciati all'orecchio. Sconto del 20% sullo store
items.summary: Gli auricolari a clip di Shokz pesano 6,4 grammi, resistono all'acqua con certificazione IP57, arrivano a 40 ore di musica con una custodia che si ricarica senza fili, e non ti isolano dal mondo. In sconto del 20% sullo store ufficiale ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Alle otto la banchina della metropolitana è piena e dall'altoparlante arriva l'annuncio di un ritardo. Chi ha gli auricolari infilati nelle orecchie se ne accorge quando il treno non arriva. Con gli OpenDots 2 di Shokz l'annuncio passa sopra la musica, perché il condotto uditivo resta libero . Gli auricolari si agganciano al bordo dell'orecchio come una clip, con l'altoparlante davanti al canale e la batteria nascosta dietro.

Sono la seconda generazione degli auricolari a clip di Shokz . Il ponte flessibile JointArc in nichel-titanio, rivestito di silicone, si adatta a orecchie di forme diverse. Ogni auricolare pesa 6,4 grammi e non ha un lato obbligato. Destro e sinistro sono intercambiabili, così di fretta si indossano senza controllare quale sia quale .

In ufficio la musica resta personale. Il sistema Bassphere 2.0 fa lavorare due driver come uno solo, con un diaframma riprogettato che riduce la distorsione del 70%.

La tecnologia MirrorPitch inclina l'uscita del suono per rifletterlo dentro l'orecchio , mentre il Dolby Audio rende più nitide le voci e più profondi i bassi.

Le telefonate di metà mattina sono il punto in cui il nuovo modello si stacca di più dagli OpenDots Air. Ogni auricolare ha tre microfoni. Due captano la voce dall'aria, il terzo è a conduzione ossea e la raccoglie dalle vibrazioni che attraversano il cranio quando si parla, un segnale che il traffico intorno disturba molto meno. Un algoritmo di intelligenza artificiale si occupa poi di filtrare il brusio di fondo .

Nella pausa pranzo si può andare in palestra senza toglierli. Gli auricolari hanno la certificazione IP57 , che oltre al sudore copre l'immersione temporanea in acqua, mentre la generazione precedente si fermava a IP55.

La giornata può finire con la custodia appoggiata su un caricatore wireless Qi , altra novità rispetto agli OpenDots Air. Gli auricolari arrivano a 10 ore di musica con una carica e a 40 complessive con la custodia. Chi si dimentica di ricaricarli recupera due ore di ascolto in cinque minuti.

Gli OpenDots 2 sono disponibili nei colori bianco, grigio e nero sullo store italiano di Shokz che attualmente prevede uno sconto del 20% rispetto al prezzo di listino . La consegna è gratuita.

items.title: Stazioni meteo per casa, quale scegliere tra sensore esterno e previsioni dalla rete. Le soluzioni Explore Scientific
items.summary: Tre stazioni Explore Scientific con sensore senza fili e una Wi-Fi che scarica le previsioni. Cosa cambia e quale scegliere, con la WSH4008C in offerta a 49,90 euro ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
In generale una stazione meteo da casa può fare due lavori diversi, e non tutte li fanno allo stesso modo. Il primo è misurare la temperatura e l'umidità dove servono, in salotto come sul balcone. Il secondo è dire che tempo farà nelle prossime ore o nei prossimi giorni.

Le stazioni con sensore esterno nascono attorno al primo compito. Misurano il microclima di casa e del giardino e ricavano la previsione dai valori che rilevano, senza bisogno di alcuna connessione. Una stazione Wi-Fi porta invece sul display le previsioni scaricate dalla rete e misura direttamente la stanza in cui si trova.

Nel catalogo di Explore Scientific ci sono entrambe le famiglie, e capire quale delle due cose interessa di più, il dato misurato o la previsione, è il modo più rapido per scegliere .

Nelle stazioni tradizionali, come la WSH4501 , la WSH4008C e la WSH4005C di Explore Scientific, il dato esterno arriva da un sensore a batterie, da sistemare sul balcone o in giardino .

Il sensore trasmette le misure alla base via radio sulla frequenza dei 433 MHz, la stessa di molti telecomandi e campanelli senza fili, quindi non serve nessun cavo e nessuna rete Wi-Fi .

La previsione la calcola la base, sui dati che raccoglie. La WSH4501 e la WSH4008C hanno anche un barometro, il sensore di pressione atmosferica, e ne mostrano il valore sul display.

Come è noto, quando la pressione cala in modo deciso di solito il tempo peggiora, quando sale tende a migliorare. Le stazioni traducono queste informazioni in un'icona, dal sole alla neve, con la previsione per le 12 ore successive.

È una previsione locale e a breve termine, calcolata su quello che succede a casa propria , ed è l'indicazione che serve per decidere se nelle prossime ore conviene ritirare i panni stesi.

La WSH4103 , la stazione smart di Explore Scientific, segue un'altra strada. Si collega alla rete Wi-Fi di casa e all'app Smart Life, basata sulla piattaforma Tuya che usano molti dispositivi per la casa connessa, e da lì scarica le previsioni della zona fino a quattro giorni insieme all'AQI, l'indice che riassume la qualità dell'aria , consultabile nell'app. Sono previsioni acquisite via Internet, che coprono più giorni e aggiungono informazioni che un barometro da solo non può fornire .

Le misure dirette riguardano invece l'interno. La WSH4103 rileva temperatura, umidità e pressione nella stanza in cui si trova .

Il display retroilluminato mostra le previsioni insieme ai valori della stanza e a un grafico a barre con l'andamento della pressione nelle ultime 12 ore . Ora e data si sincronizzano da sole tramite l'app.

Non mancano le funzioni di tutti i giorni. C'è una sveglia con snooze di 5 minuti, che si ferma da sola dopo due minuti se nessuno la spegne. Un indicatore di comfort incrocia temperatura e umidità e segnala con un'icona se l'aria in casa è troppo secca o troppo umida.

Si collega alle reti Wi-Fi a 2,4 GHz e funziona con l'alimentatore incluso, mentre due batterie AA mantengono l'ora se si stacca la corrente. Colore disponibile, solo nero.

La WSH4501 ha un display LCD semitrasparente in vetro , una soluzione che la fa somigliare più a un oggetto d'arredamento che a uno strumento, ed è disponibile in bianco o in nero. Nella confezione c'è un sensore per temperatura e umidità esterne, e la base ne gestisce fino a tre .

Come la WSH4103, ha la sveglia con snooze di 5 minuti e l'indicatore di comfort. A queste aggiunge le funzioni legate alle misure dirette. Il display mostra la pressione atmosferica, in hPa o in pollici di mercurio, e la previsione per le 12 ore successive con cinque icone .

L'orologio è radiocontrollato e segnala l'ora legale, e si possono impostare avvisi di massima e di minima sulla temperatura esterna, canale per canale. Funziona con due batterie AAA, incluse insieme a quelle del sensore. Colore disponibile, solo bianco.

La WSH4008C è il modello più conveniente in questi giorni. Fino al 29 novembre costa 49,90 euro invece di 64,99 .

Il display a colori è un pannello VA retroilluminato , una tecnologia LCD che offre un buon contrasto, con la luminosità regolabile. Accanto all'ora e al calendario mostra la pressione atmosferica con il trend barometrico, cioè se la pressione sta salendo o scendendo, insieme a una previsione per le 12 ore successive con sei icone e alle fasi lunari.

Si possono impostare avvisi di massima e di minima sia sulla temperatura esterna sia su quella interna , per esempio per sapere quando di notte si scende sotto lo zero e conviene ritirare le piante dal balcone.

La WSH4005C è l'unica che include tre sensori esterni , ciascuno con una portata di 30 metri e un proprio canale. Il display a colori mostra le misure della base e quelle di ciascun sensore , che può restare fuori oppure finire nella camera dei bambini o in cantina.

La base conserva i valori massimi e minimi di temperatura e umidità, e una freccia indica se la temperatura è salita o scesa rispetto a tre ore prima. La previsione copre le 12 ore successive con sei icone.

L'orologio è radiocontrollato e cerca il segnale ogni notte finché non si sincronizza. Come sugli altri modelli c'è la sveglia, con snooze di 5 minuti.

Si alimenta con tre batterie AAA oppure con l'alimentatore da 5 V, entrambi nella confezione insieme alle batterie dei sensori . Con l'alimentatore la retroilluminazione resta accesa e si regola su due livelli o si spegne. Colori disponibili, bianco e nero.

Chi vuole sapere quanti gradi ci sono davvero sul balcone deve partire da una delle tre stazioni con sensore. La WSH4501 basta se serve un solo punto di misura e un oggetto discreto ed elegante da appoggiare sulla mensola, con sveglia e avvisi di temperatura già a bordo.

La WSH4008C costa pochi euro in più in questa settimana e aggiunge il display a colori, il trend della pressione e gli avvisi anche sulla temperatura interna, con l'alimentatore nella confezione.

Se le stanze da controllare sono più di una, la WSH4005C le copre già dalla confezione con tre sensori.

Per chi invece vuole sapere che tempo farà domani e dopodomani, e magari tenere d'occhio la qualità dell'aria, la scelta giusta è la WSH4103 , l'unica delle quattro che scarica le previsioni dalla rete e si controlla anche dallo smartphone.

Tutti e quattro i modelli si acquistano sul sito di Explore Scientific. L'offerta sulla WSH4008C a 49,90 euro resta valida fino al 29 novembre .

items.title: La palestra di casa cambia forma: con Speediance pesi, cyclette e personal trainer diventano digitali
items.summary: Niente pile di dischi, niente muri da forare e molto più software. Tutto converge verso una palestra domestica sempre più connessa: e per il Black Friday gli sconti arrivano a 500 euro ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Una palestra in casa, fino a qualche anno fa, significava soprattutto trovare spazio. Per il rack, per i dischi, per il bilanciere, per una panca; magari per una macchina a cavi e, se rimanevano ancora alcuni metri quadrati liberi, anche per una cyclette. Tantissimo spazio: per molte persone significava non farcela e rinunciare ad avere un allenamento completo fra le mura della propria abitazione.

Per riuscire a soddisfare questa esigenza, Speediance è partita dalla domanda opposta: quanta di quella meccanica può essere sostituita dalla tecnologia?

Così, al posto di una pila di pesi ci sono motori digitali che generano una resistenza controllata dal software; invece di cambiare dischi si modifica il carico dallo schermo, anche mezzo chilogrammo alla volta.

Un personal trainer digitale può costruire il programma e seguire l'allenamento, mentre dispositivi indossabili e applicazioni raccolgono informazioni che aiutano a capire non soltanto quanto ci si è allenati, ma anche come si sta recuperando.

È questo che rende speciale la gamma Speediance: rendere digitale ciò che normalmente in palestra è meccanico e riunire in un ecosistema elementi che solitamente vivono separati. Con l’aggiunta di un’installazione così semplice da essere rivoluzionaria . Il risultato non è una palestra tradizionale semplicemente rimpicciolita, è un'altra interpretazione della home gym.

Per il Black Friday, in più, Speediance ha previsto fino a 500 euro di sconto sulle sue macchine più performanti .

La parte interessante, per una casa, è che le macchine di Speediance, come Gym Monster 3 e Gym Monster 2S, non richiedono di trasformare definitivamente una stanza in palestra. La struttura, infatti, è autoportante: non bisogna fissarla alla parete né praticare fori .

Inoltre, quando l’allenamento è finito la struttura può essere ripiegata , così da occupare meno spazio.

Usando come esempio la Gym Monster 3, una volta aperta misura 122 × 69 × 185 cm e occupa circa 0,84 metri quadrati durante l'allenamento; terminata la sessione, la pedana può essere richiusa e la profondità scende da 122 a 37 cm, con un ingombro a pavimento di circa 0,25 metri quadrati.

Quindi, in altre parole, si posiziona la macchina, la si alimenta e si può iniziare a configurarla. Tutto qui. Il peso della macchina è comunque importante, circa 82 kg nel caso della Gym Monster 3, ma una volta installata non bisogna circondarla permanentemente di dischi, rack e altre macchine.

Inoltre, anche durante l'uso, e proprio grazie all'adozione di un sistema elettronico, le macchine di Speediance non sono come le altre: sono silenziosissime . La rumorosità della smart bike Velonix, per esempio, è inferiore ai 50 dB(A). Può essere usata quindi in una stanza dove ci sono altre persone senza creare alcun disturbo.

Gym Monster 3 è proprio il prodotto esemplificativo per spiegare come funziona, nella pratica, l'approccio studiato da Speediance. Osservando questa macchina non si notano pacchi pesi né una rastrelliera piena di dischi, perché la resistenza viene generata da due motori direct-drive sincroni da 800 W , capaci di arrivare complessivamente a 100 kg: 50 kg per ciascun lato. Il carico può essere regolato con incrementi di 0,5 kg.

Con un peso tradizionale, 30 kg rimangono 30 kg per tutta la ripetizione. Il motore, invece, permette di gestire il comportamento dei 30 kg di resistenza durante l'allenamento, scegliendo tra quattro diverse modalità:

Lo stesso hardware può assumere così comportamenti differenti senza aggiungere o rimuovere fisicamente nulla. L’utente deve solo pensare a come vuole allenarsi e la macchina viene adattata velocemente alle esigenze.

In più, le 19 posizioni dei cavi, distanziate di 7,5 cm, ampliano le possibilità di configurazione, permettendo di modificare altezza e angolo della trazione. Una sola macchina raccoglie in un unico sistema esercizi e funzionalità normalmente associati a cable trainer, squat rack, Smith machine, ski machine, bilanciere, manubri e leg curl machine.

In più, attraverso l'assistenza virtuale Aevis è possibile interagire con il sistema usando solo i comandi vocali e senza usare le mani. Così, se serve ridurre la resistenza basta chiederlo ad Aevis, che reagisce subisce modificando la configurazione.

E durante l'utilizzo, subentra la modalità Spotter: monitora la velocità dei movimenti in tempo reale e se rileva un calo delle prestazioni, riduce la resistenza per evitare di sovraccaricare l'esercizio e permettere di completarlo in sicurezza.

Gym Monster 3 viene proposta in più configurazioni, ma è importante chiarire che non cambia la macchina alla base: cambiano gli accessori compresi nella confezione.

La versione Studio aggiunge al kit standard la panca inclinabile , ampliando gli esercizi che possono essere eseguiti seduti o distesi.

La versione Station parte dalla stessa Gym Monster 3 e comprende a sua volta la panca inclinabile, ma aggiunge anche AeroRow Bench e Rowing Bar. In pratica, alla parte dedicata alla forza affianca una configurazione completa per il vogatore , sfruttando la resistenza digitale della macchina anche per il movimento di remata. Non aumentano potenza dei motori o carico massimo.

Perciò la scelta tra Studio e Station dipende meno dal livello di forza dell'utente e più da ciò che si vuole fare con la macchina. Studio è la configurazione pensata soprattutto per allenamento di forza e workout con la panca; Station aggiunge il necessario per integrare anche il rowing nello stesso ecosistema.

Per il Black Friday, Gym Monster 3 Studio è in offerta a 4.199 euro anziché 4.699 euro. La versione Station invece è scontata a 4.599 euro anziché 5.099 euro.

Sul sito di Speediance è disponibile anche la Gym Monster 3S . Parte dalla stessa architettura di Gym Monster 3, ma aumenta soprattutto la capacità del sistema di resistenza.

I due motori passano da 800 a 1.000 W ciascuno e il carico digitale massimo sale da 100 a 120 kg complessivi, cioè fino a 60 kg per lato. Anche qui la regolazione avviene con incrementi di 0,5 kg.

Dimensioni e filosofia rimangono sostanzialmente invariate: 122 x 69 x 185 cm da aperto, 37 x 69 x 185 cm da chiuso, 19 posizioni per i cavi e le stesse quattro modalità Standard, Eccentrica, Catena e Velocità fissa. Il peso sale leggermente, a circa 86 kg.

Gym Monster 2S porta la stessa idea della resistenza digitale verso carichi ancora più elevati. Due motori direct-drive PMSM da 800 W sostituiscono ancora una volta il tradizionale pacco pesi, ma la resistenza massima arriva a 120 kg complessivi, circa 60 kg per lato, con regolazioni fino a 0,5 kg.

Rimangono le quattro modalità che caratterizzano l'approccio Speediance. Standard mantiene costante il peso selezionato; Eccentrica aumenta il carico nella fase negativa della ripetizione; Catena fa crescere progressivamente la resistenza lungo il movimento; Velocità fissa permette invece di controllarne il ritmo.

Gym Monster 2S aggiunge anche Safety Start, che permette di definire una zona nella quale la resistenza entra in funzione e di rilasciarla quando il movimento supera determinati limiti. I sensori controllano il movimento e il sistema può interrompere rapidamente la resistenza quando rileva una situazione non sicura .

La piattaforma integra poi uno schermo touch Full HD da 21,5 pollici, orientabile tra 0 e 90 gradi, dal quale si gestiscono allenamenti, carico e programmi.

L'altezza dei punti di trazione può essere regolata su 11 livelli e anche Gym Monster 2S nasce come soluzione autoportante: non richiede fori, montaggio a parete o un'installazione permanente nella stanza.

Anche Gym Monster 2S è disponibile in due versioni: Work Plus e Family Plus.

Gym Monster 2S Work Plus abbina alla macchina il set di accessori necessario per sfruttare le differenti configurazioni dei cavi e, soprattutto, una panca regolabile. Quest’ultima è ciò che trasforma concretamente molte delle possibilità della macchina: permette di passare dagli esercizi in piedi a distensioni, alzate, row, curl e movimenti eseguiti in posizione seduta, prona o supina, modificandone anche l’inclinazione.

Nel corredo della 2S ci sono Bluetooth Ring, corda per tricipiti, cavigliere, tappetino, bilanciere regolabile, imbottitura e ganci per il bilanciere, cinghie di estensione, adattatore angolare e PowerGrip.

Family Plus mantiene quanto previsto da Work Plus, compresa la panca regolabile, ma aggiunge una seconda panca dedicata al rowing. In pratica, in questa configurazione, Gym Monster 2S può essere usare anche come vogatore .

La resistenza necessaria alla remata continua a essere generata digitalmente dalla Gym Monster; la Rowing Bench fornisce invece la posizione e il movimento necessari per trasformare i cavi in un sistema dedicato al rowing aerobico. La macchina dispone anche di un punto specifico per il collegamento della configurazione da vogatore, pensato per rendere più controllato il movimento.

Per il Black Friday, Gym Monster 2S Work Plus è scontata a 4.409,99 euro anziché 4.899,99 euro. Mentre la versione Family Plus è proposta a 4.809,99 euro invece che 5.299,99 euro.

items.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
items.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
items.content:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.

"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."

The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

items.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
items.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
items.content:
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.

In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.

"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.

Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"

When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.

"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.

Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.

Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a tradition that blends music and dance, with lyrics that can be bawdy or politically incisive, set to the rhythms of a double-headed drum called the dholki.

Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.

"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.

Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.

It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.

Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.

Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.

Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.

At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.

There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.

In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.

When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.

Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.

Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.

Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.

Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.

Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.

Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.

Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.

Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.

"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.

But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.

"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

items.title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
items.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
items.content:
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.

Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.

When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.

Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.

Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.

"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.

The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.

But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.

"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.

"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."

Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.

During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.

"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."

It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.

"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.

"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.

The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.

"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."

In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.

Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.

"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.

Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.

Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

items.title: Lagioia: “Non mi scandalizzo, i miei romanzi sono già schedati ma temo chi controlla i sistemi”
items.summary: Il punto è che un mezzo così potente è in mano a pochi privati. In una democrazia dovrebbe essere nazionalizzata
items.content:
I suoi libri, racconta, sono già finiti negli archivi usati per addestrare l’intelligenza artificiale. Eppure Nicola Lagioia, premio Strega con La ferocia e autore di Santa Barbara (Einaudi), non teme le macchine che scrivono romanzi. Piuttosto, che l’IA cambi il nostro modo di pensare.

«Perché la questione è più profonda: come la tecnologia cambia la mente umana. Stiamo esternalizzando tutto, l’orientamento a Google Maps, la memoria al telefonino. Dai tempi di Sant’Agostino parliamo con una voce interiore che chiamiamo Io , gli antichi la attribuivano agli dei. Adesso lo facciamo sempre di più con l’IA. La nostra voce interiore cambierà, e con lei il pensiero. Chi scriverà romanzi non avrà la stessa mente di Tolstoj, Proust o Virginia Woolf. Siamo una specie che si automodifica con gli strumenti e gli utensili che inventa. È un processo che, di nuovo, sta accadendo con la tecnologia. Non sappiamo bene in che cosa ci stiamo trasformando, ma in fondo non lo sapevamo nemmeno prima».

«È già così. I miei, come quelli di tutti noi. Tempo fa andai a controllare su un sito che elencava i titoli dati in pasto alla macchina. Negli Stati Uniti non sono un autore famoso, eppure nella lista c’ero anche io».

Il libro è un oggetto. Cosa si perde se ne resta solo il testo?

«La letteratura ha cambiato supporto molte volte. La pietra, i papiri, i codici, la galassia Gutenberg, poi il digitale. L’hardware del linguaggio è la mente umana, non il supporto».

Eppure qui i libri verrebbero poi tagliati, scansionati e mandati al macero.

«Non mi sembra la cosa peggiore. È come se stesse arrivando, o fosse già arrivata, un’inondazione e noi ci preoccupassimo di un singolo filo d’erba spezzato».

«A me preoccupa molto di più l’uso dell’IA in guerra che in letteratura. Occuparsi tanto dei romanzi e così poco di come viene usata per sterminare le persone è una distrazione che non mi piace. Da scrittore, quello della letteratura mi sembra un falso problema».

«Le big tech sono un problema politico, e non solo per l’IA. Non pagano le tasse. Violano le leggi. Visto che ci avviciniamo alle elezioni, mi aspetterei che entrambi gli schieramenti ci dicessero che cosa vogliono fare con queste multinazionali che usano il loro potere in modo spregiudicato».

Sceglie le parole in maniera precisa. Si dice spesso che i libri “nutrano” l’IA. Una metafora giusta?

«Nutrendo, cioè perfezionando, questo strumento, modifichiamo noi stessi. Mi interessa l’uomo, la macchina conta solo per come lo modifica. Il punto è che un mezzo così potente è in mano a pochi privati. In una democrazia, l’intelligenza artificiale la nazionalizzerei».

Perciò se i suoi libri servissero alla pubblica utilità, le andrebbe bene?

«Se ne fossi sicuro, sarei contento. Il punto è che non è così. Il timore è che possano servire, i miei come quelli di centinaia di migliaia di altri scrittori, a trovare formule retoriche per cambiare l’esito delle elezioni, per fare propaganda, per individuare i ricercati in guerra e colpirli, per la profilazione razziale. Questo mi farebbe orrore».

items.title: Italy’s best building is a gateway to the afterlife
items.summary: The new entrance to Naples’ Fontanelle Cemetery has won the prestigious architecture prize awarded by MAXXI and Triennale, bringing a centuries-old tradition of popular devotion into the future
items.content:
Italy’s best architectural project of the year is in Naples, and it is a place where the worlds of the living and the dead meet. The 2026 Italian Architecture Prize, promoted by Rome’s MAXXI and Milan’s Triennale, has gone to the redevelopment of the entrance to the Fontanelle Cemetery and its surrounding public spaces. The historic ossuary is carved into volcanic tuff deep within the labyrinthine streets of the Rione Sanità district.

The award, presented on 15 November at MAXXI in Rome, follows another recognition: the national IN/ARCHITETTURA Prize for urban regeneration, presented two days earlier at the headquarters of the Venice Biennale.

Behind the project is a team of architects under 35 – Marino Amodio, Giuseppe De Pascale, Orazio Nicodemo and Davide Savoia – coordinated by Daniela Buonanno and Nicola Flora, architecture professors at Naples’ Federico II University. The project was developed under the guidance of internationally renowned architect Renzo Piano, who funds scholarships for the young architects with his salary as a senator for life.

The jury recognised the innovative scope of a project that enhances one of the sanctuaries of Neapolitan popular devotion. Naples has developed an entire cult around the thousands of anonymous skulls that populate the Fontanelle, the so-called anime pezzentelle , or poor souls. These dispossessed inhabitants of the afterlife are tormented spirits whom worshippers welcome into their family pantheon alongside their own loved ones. The forgiving outlook on life that characterises Neapolitan ethics thus extends into the next world, turning it into an otherworldly reflection of the city’s bustling communitas , sustained by a constant exchange of favours, goods and care between the two worlds.

In essence, this Neapolitan cult appeals to a tangible form of mercy, a flesh-and-blood compassion for what Baudelaire, in a moving sonnet from The Flowers of Evil , calls the sorrows of the dead: “The dead, the poor dead, have great sorrows.” People adopt these remains as though they were foundlings, pray for them, give them names and enter them into the civil registry of eternity. Indeed, this form of compassion, embracing both the living and the dead, is the cornerstone of Neapolitan culture and its deeply humane religion, woven around an intense and uninterrupted dialogue with the departed, who often become guardians of the fortunes of the living, guiding their moral choices and destinies.

Poems such as Totò’s ’A livella ( The Spirit Level ) and plays such as Eduardo De Filippo’s Questi fantasmi ( These Ghosts ) and Le voci di dentro ( Inner Voices ) make the departed the ultimate custodians and guarantors of the values and actions of the living. The cult of the souls inhabiting the Fontanelle thus goes far beyond paying tribute to deceased loved ones, extending an extraordinarily humane and civilised form of care to the unknown multitudes of the poor in the afterlife.

Today, this phenomenon, which many regarded as a fragment of the past destined to become obsolete, has been revived thanks to the young people of La Paranza, a social cooperative in the Rione Sanità inspired by the spiritual guidance of Father Antonio Loffredo. Credit also goes to Naples City Council, which recognised the potential of a tradition capable of reconnecting past and future. The award-winning project translates that connection into physical spaces where the mysterious, silent shadows of this neighbourhood underworld meet the bustling, sunlit city.

As a result, the Fontanelle Cemetery has become a magnet for curious and reflective travellers, giving rise to new rituals. A particularly moving one centres on the body of a little girl kept in a glass case at the entrance to the cemetery. Schoolchildren visiting the ossuary leave sweets, little toys, hairbands, colourful hairpins, bracelets and messages for the child whose life was cut short.

What generations of Neapolitans regarded as the gates of Hades, open to crowds of worshippers who could make the “inner voices” resonate, now welcomes throngs of visitors drawn to this theatre of mercy. Here, in stark contrast to contemporary society’s tendency to deny death, they discover a way of rethinking it as part of life.

In this timeless ossuary, visitors experience what the Italian poet Ugo Foscolo, in Of Tombs , calls a “correspondence of loving feelings”. A sense of closeness to those who have gone but have not abandoned us. It is precisely the secret of this closeness that people come here to discover.

items.title: Villa featured in Oscar-nominated film The Spiral goes on the market for €4 million
items.summary: In the province of Bari, buyers can purchase the 1,400-square-metre property, complete with marble staircases and a landscaped park with a swimming pool, which served as a location for Paolo Strippoli’s film. “The ending is still waiting to be written,” jokes the estate agent
items.content:
“What if the next story set in this villa were yours?” It would take “just” €4 million to buy the property in Gioia del Colle chosen as a location for Paolo Strippoli’s Oscar-nominated film The Spiral .

The listing, published by estate agency Coldwell Banker, describes the historic villa as “a residence of rare beauty, combining the charm of the past with the comforts of contemporary living”.

The 1,400-square-metre property is spread over two floors. According to the listing, it represents “an example of architectural and residential excellence, ideal for those seeking an exclusive setting surrounded by elegance, privacy and nature”.

It boasts six bedrooms, a fireplace and nine bathrooms, as well as a games room with a pool table, a private study and a library in a classic style. There is also a “spacious main reception room, enhanced by fine finishes and opening onto a beautiful covered loggia, alongside two inviting living rooms on a raised level, accessed via an impressive double marble staircase that lends the space a timeless, theatrical elegance”.

The icing on the cake? Ten thousand square metres of landscaped grounds, complete with a manicured lawn, a 150-square-metre swimming pool and a sports court suitable for tennis, padel or five-a-side football.

“The quality of the materials, the architectural attention to detail and the atmosphere of a bygone era,” the listing continues, “make this villa in Gioia del Colle a one-of-a-kind property, perfect as a prestigious family home or an impressive residence for entertaining”.

“It is no coincidence that the estate has been chosen as a set for several films and commercials, a testament to its extraordinary beauty and distinctive character”.

The agency’s website allows prospective buyers not only to book a viewing but also to take a virtual tour of the property.

“The real plot twist in The Spiral isn’t the film itself,” says Pier Panessa, the estate agent handling the sale, “but the fact that this villa is on the market. Now the ending could be anyone’s to write.”

items.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
items.summary: Article URL: https://research.google/blog/supercharging-transformer-residual-connections/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50672565 Points: 306 # Comments: 126
items.content:
Kyriakos Axiotis, Staff Research Scientist, and Thomas Fu, Principal Engineer, Google Research

We present DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architecture that enhances transformer networks by using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to dynamically combine outputs from previous layers, preventing the information dilution seen in traditional residual connections. Presented in our ICML 2025 paper, this architectural improvement allows models to achieve the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters.

Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections , also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections ," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

Instead of treating skip connections as a rigid, additive pipeline, DCA reframes residual learning as a dynamic routing problem. Rather than passing all prior layers forward with equal weight, DCA introduces a lightweight, layer-wise module that decides how to best combine previous embeddings on a per-token basis.

Comparison between a standard residual network and DeepCrossAttention (DCA). While a standard residual network uses rigid, additive point-wise connections with equal weighting, DCA introduces dynamic, learned routing weights (W) that allow each layer to selectively route and combine features from across the history of preceding layers.

By allowing the network to dynamically select and retrieve high-resolution features from earlier layers, DCA eliminates the information dilution inherent to classic residual connections.

To test whether DCA can overcome information dilution in practice, we evaluated our approach across controlled synthetic setups, large-scale language modeling benchmarks, and image classification tasks.

DCA demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed, training stability, and final model quality across these experiments.

Perplexity (PPL) — how well a probability model predicts a sample — comparison across language modeling benchmarks. On both the LM1B (top) and C4 (bottom) datasets, DeepCrossAttention (DCA) achieves lower perplexity than standard transformers and alternative connection baselines (such as LAUREL-PA, 1x1-DenseFormer, and Hyper-Connections) under the same parameter and training budgets.

On the colossal, cleaned version of Common Crawl's web crawl corpus (C4) and 1 Billion Word Language Model Benchmark ( LM1B ) datasets, DCA reached the performance of standard transformers in up to five times fewer training steps. When trained for the same duration or number of steps, DCA consistently achieved lower perplexity — how well a probability model predicts a sample — than standard residual connections, effectively extracting more representational capacity from the same training budget. To achieve a perplexity of <14 on LM1B, a standard transformer with fixed width required 42 layers, whereas the DCA model achieved a lower perplexity with only 30 layers — a 29% reduction in depth and parameter count.

Impact of varying connection history (k) on model perplexity. Performance comparison showing how scaling the number of preceding layer connections in DCA consistently improves language modeling perplexity over the standard Transformer baseline, achieving the lowest perplexity at higher configurations (16-DCA and 24-DCA).

One of the most common trade-offs in AI is that better models are often much larger and slower to run. DCA adds a tiny number of parameters — less than 0.2% of the total model size — making it negligible in terms of compute and memory footprint, while increasing memory bandwidth, as representations from different layers are presented intact rather than blended together. Interestingly, because DCA can be initialized to behave identically to a standard residual network, it doesn’t require training from scratch: retrofitting DCA onto an already pre-trained transformer and briefly continuing training reduced perplexity by 0.19 on LM1B, compared to just 0.02 for continued standard training.

As large language models (LLMs) are used across a broader range of domains, optimizing their training processes and underlying architectures is critical for scaling and unlocking new capabilities. DCA and similar dynamic residual techniques are already seeing significant adoption and success. The rapid emergence of these methodologies highlights dynamic routing as a highly active and promising area of research.

Developed by Moonshot AI, attention residuals share DCA's core principles of replacing fixed addition with selective retrieval. Instead of blindly summing every prior layer's output, they use a learnable softmax attention mechanism paired with a layer-specific pseudo-query. This allows each layer to selectively weight and retrieve representations from earlier depths. By preventing the unbounded growth of hidden states and the dilution of early-layer information, this method improves gradient stability and boosts performance on reasoning-heavy tasks like coding and mathematics. To maintain computational efficiency at scale, a "Block AttnRes" variant partitions layers into blocks, recovering the benefits of full attention with significantly less memory overhead. The recent Inkling 2 model developed by Thinking Machines also adopted this design in addition to DCA’s cross attention (Q/K/V split) mechanism.

Hyper-connections expand the residual stream into multiple parallel channels, offering a form of memory scaling that goes beyond simply increasing model width or depth. They use a fixed-size stack where layer outputs are aggregated and mixed using learnable mixing matrices. However, this unconstrained mixing breaks the traditional identity mapping property of residual connections, which can cause amplification or attenuation of signals, and lead to training instability at scale.

To address instability in standard hyper-connections, manifold-constrained hyper-connections apply specific constraints to the mixing matrices. By forcing these matrices to live on a defined manifold — specifically, constraining them to be doubly stochastic using the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm — manifold-constrained hyper-connections restore stable signal propagation. This approach prevents exploding or vanishing gradients while preserving the rich information flow and expressivity of the widened residual streams, allowing models to scale robustly.

DCA demonstrates that transitioning from static residual connections to dynamic, attention-based routing is a powerful strategy for building more efficient models. By leveraging an expanded residual stream and depth-wise cross-attention, DCA empowers deep networks to selectively retrieve and integrate token embeddings across different layers. We expect that next-generation models will dynamically route and weigh past layer representations based on the specific tokens or inputs being processed. This will allow for the effective use of all the model layers as specialized experts working in tandem, with maximum information sharing and no redundancy, leading to more expressivity and deeper interactions. We look forward to seeing how these multi-depth interactions will shape the next generation of transformer architectures.

items.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
items.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
items.content:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.

"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.

"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."

When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".

"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.

"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."

These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.

Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."

The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns: dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiananmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after. More recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.

Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."

items.title: Tabernetes: A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs
items.summary: Article URL: https://tabernet.es/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50672521 Points: 90 # Comments: 32
items.content:
Open the page and your phone is a node. The scheduler sends it a pod, and the pod's program runs on a Linux kernel booted in the tab. Close the tab and the node is gone, and Kubernetes starts the pod on someone else's.

Scan to become a node , or use the browser you are reading this in.

Joining downloads about 5 MB and runs a small Linux guest in the tab, on one core, until you close the tab.

The control plane in the middle, a node for each tab, and each Service on the way to the pods behind it. A node is filled when its pod is running. An orange dot is a request you sent, on its way to the pod that answered, and a green one is a tile of the picture on its way to the node that rendered it.

How long a tab takes to start its pod: from the tab being handed the pod to the pod's program running, which is the page loading, the kernel booting and the image being mounted. The last 0 starts.

How long the cluster takes to answer: from the agent handing a request to the Service to the answer being back from a pod in someone's tab, timed on the cluster's machine. The last 0 requests, from every visitor, by the milliseconds each took.

Send a request to a Service. One of the pods behind it answers, on whoever's phone that is, and counts the visit in a Redis on someone else's.

Press the button and the cluster draws a Mandelbrot set. The picture is split into 64 tiles, and each node's pod computes its share in awk, on the Linux in its tab. Point at a tile to see which device drew it.

The cluster's Services that have a pod on a tab behind them, read from the API server.

The control plane is an ordinary Kubernetes, and a pod is an ordinary pod. The marked line is the only one that is new: the scheduler puts a pod that has it on a tab, and every other pod on the cluster's own machine.

items.title: Source Control from Hell
items.summary: Article URL: https://frantic.im/git/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50672142 Points: 84 # Comments: 62
items.content:
My first office job was at an enterprise that built software for a big telecom: a massive Delphi help desk application on Windows.

Let me tell you about how we managed source control process at the time.

First, you download the code from a shared folder (hosted on a trusted Windows server in a locked room). Build your thing, run the app, test it locally. Then you upload your changes to the shared folder and create a new ticket in the internal task tracker (also a Windows app). The ticket should have a list of the changes you’ve made, in a rich text editor, in a manual format somewhat resembling a patch. But it wasn’t a patch; it couldn’t simply be applied with a tool. Instead, the tech lead looks at the shared folder and your task and copies the relevant changes to his own integration folder. This usually took him a full day because the shared folder had a lot of changes, not all of them were ready to be integrated. Needless to say, if you simply pull a snapshot of the code from the shared folder, it would most likely fail to compile.

The most common problem was two people overwriting each other’s work. So if you wanted to upload your stuff to the shared folder, you had to stand up and announce in a loud voice that you were using the shared folder. No chat apps back in the day.

Imagine starting your career with this development experience! I did my best to improve it. At the time, almost everyone used FAR Manager , so I built a plugin that locked the folder when someone was using it, so others would get a warning. It became very popular because nobody really liked the old yelling system.

Then in 2009 I found git. It was still early days, way before GitHub went mainstream, but my tiny little brain was blown away. Holy shit, it maintains old versions. And you can work locally. And you can sync and exchange deltas. And it was insanely fast (compared to the very aptly named TortoiseSVN I’d experimented with earlier). I must have rewatched Linus’ talk a billion times. I created git repos for every project I had, preached it to my friends, and even gave my first tech talk about git at my university.

Sadly, my diplomatic skills were extremely rudimentary, and I couldn’t convince our tech lead to adopt git. He mumbled something about business value and how this new git thing lacked one. I left the company after two years but kept meeting up with old colleagues for beer. They were still using the shared folder process many years later. It was crude, it was hellish, and it worked for them just fine.
